papers.title: The Transformer Cookbook
papers.authors: Andy Yang, Christopher Watson, Anton Xue, Satwik Bhattamishra, Jose Llarena, William Merrill, Emile Dos Santos Ferreira, Anej Svete, and David Chiang
papers.standfirst: A collection of recipes for turning algorithms into transformer weights.
summary: This paper brings together techniques for explicitly constructing transformers that carry out algorithms. Its recipes cover arithmetic in feed-forward layers and routing information through attention.

The collection offers a shared reference for constructions scattered across the literature. It is a useful place to begin when you want to understand how a computation can be represented inside the architecture.
papers.whyRead: For the moment when you want to build a transformer construction, and need a place to start.
readingGuide: Choose one operation you already understand and follow how the paper encodes it.
Keep track of the architectural assumptions each recipe needs before combining constructions.
papers.caveat: An explicit construction describes what chosen parameters can compute. Whether training discovers those parameters is a separate question.

papers.title: What Formal Languages Can Transformers Express? A Survey
papers.authors: Lena Strobl, William Merrill, Gail Weiss, David Chiang, and Dana Angluin
papers.standfirst: A map of expressivity results—and the assumptions that make them fit together.
summary: The survey organizes theoretical work on which formal languages transformers can recognize. It documents the assumptions behind different results and provides a framework for comparing findings that can initially seem contradictory.
For a reader moving between papers, this is an entry point into the vocabulary of the area: what a result says depends on which transformer model it studies.
papers.whyRead: For reading two apparently contradictory results and figuring out which assumptions changed.
readingGuide: Start with the definitions of the computational models before comparing their language classes.
Use the references to follow one expressivity question into its original proofs.
papers.caveat: A survey is a map of the literature at its publication date. Check the original paper for the exact statement and assumptions of any theorem you plan to use.

papers.title: Thinking Like Transformers
papers.authors: Gail Weiss, Yoav Goldberg, and Eran Yahav
papers.standfirst: A programming language for reasoning about transformer computation.
summary: The paper introduces RASP, the Restricted Access Sequence Processing language. It turns elements of transformer-encoder computation into primitives that can be composed into understandable programs.
Examples include histograms, sorting, and Dyck languages. The abstraction lets readers connect a task's program to the attention heads and layers needed to express it.
papers.whyRead: For thinking through a transformer algorithm as a program you can inspect, one step at a time.
readingGuide: Work through a small RASP program with a short input sequence before moving to a larger example.
Notice which operations are sequence-wise computations and which select information from other positions.
papers.caveat: A hand-written program is an abstraction of a possible computation, not evidence that every trained transformer uses that program.
